task_row_model.query: In a randomized controlled trial that shows baseline imbalance in known prognostic covariates, what should be the prespecified primary analysis to give unbiased estimates and valid inference, and which sensitivity analyses should be prespecified to assess robustness and correct Type I error?

documents.content: Academic excerpt: Contemporary trial methodology recommends specifying an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) as the primary efficacy model when baseline prognostic covariates are imbalanced or strongly predictive of outcome. ANCOVA models include the randomized treatment indicator plus baseline covariates (including stratification factors) as regressors; this preserves unbiased treatment estimates under randomization and increases precision. Investigators should prespecify which baseline covariates will be adjusted for and report adjusted point estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values. Failure to adjust for stratification factors can alter variance estimates; therefore adjustment for factors used in randomization is standard practice in primary analyses.
documents.reasoning_trace: Included ANCOVA, adjustment for baseline and stratification covariates, prespecification, and effect on variance/precision.

documents.content: Journalistic-methods brief: Trialists are advised to analyze trials by the intention-to-treat principle as the default primary approach, analyzing participants in their randomized groups regardless of adherence. For small trials or when distributional assumptions are questionable, randomization-based inference such as permutation tests that preserve the original randomization scheme can provide valid Type I error control. Such tests should respect stratification or blocking used at randomization. The brief emphasized that the primary analysis be laid out in the protocol and statistical analysis plan before unblinding.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provided intention-to-treat as primary principle and randomization-based permutation tests for small samples; noted preserving stratification and prespecification.

documents.content: Investigator notes (informal): Sensitivity analyses commonly prespecified include an unadjusted comparison of outcomes by randomized group to show robustness of adjusted results; a covariate-adjusted model using robust/heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors; analyses handling missing data such as multiple imputation under plausible missingness models; and per-protocol or complier analyses labeled explicitly as sensitivity or secondary because they may be biased. For small samples, repeating inference with permutation tests that maintain the randomization structure is also recommended as a robustness check.
documents.reasoning_trace: Listed sensitivity analyses: unadjusted, adjusted with robust SEs, multiple imputation for missing data, per-protocol as sensitivity, and permutation tests for small samples.

documents.content: Reference entry (historical/adjacent): Randomized trials trace back to early 20th-century public health interventions and later to mid-century clinical experiments; methodological discussions often include debates about intention-to-treat versus per-protocol, p-hacking concerns, and the rise of CONSORT reporting. Some texts add case studies from crossover and animal studies that are not directly analogous to parallel-group RCTs. Standard glossary entries define stratification, blocking, and prognostic covariate, and provide background on effect modification and interaction testing as separate exploratory analyses.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provided domain background and unrelated historical/case study noise; not used for core recommendations.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Prespecify an intention-to-treat primary analysis using ANCOVA: a regression of outcome on randomized treatment plus baseline prognostic covariates and any stratification factors to preserve unbiased estimates and improve precision. Prespecify sensitivity analyses: unadjusted comparison, covariate-adjusted models with robust standard errors, multiple imputation for missing data, and randomization-preserving permutation tests (especially in small samples).
